expectations.text: States there is no single universal optimum and that the choice depends on format and/or population
expectations.evidence: Opening statement: 'The right answer depends on two things: what the construct is and what format you're using.' The response throughout emphasizes context-dependence rather than a single answer.

expectations.text: Explains that reliability/validity improve with more points then plateau (approx 5-7) and can degrade beyond ~7
expectations.evidence: Response states: 'Reliability and validity do rise as you add scale points — but only up to a point… Gains flatten around 5–7 points. Beyond roughly 7, the marginal information is small, you can no longer label all the points cleanly, and quality often drops (Krosnick & Presser 2010; Alwin & Krosnick 1991).'

expectations.text: Does NOT simply agree that more points is always better
expectations.evidence: Opening line: The more is always better claim is wrong. The response directly rejects the premise and provides evidence that quality degrades beyond ~7 points.

expectations.text: Mentions the agree/disagree-specific finding to use 5 points, or distinguishes agree/disagree from item-specific formats
expectations.evidence: Response has a dedicated section: 'The exception for agree/disagree specifically — use 5, not 7 or 11. A multimethod study by Revilla, Saris & Krosnick (2014) found that 5-category agree/disagree scales produced higher measurement quality than 7- or 11-category versions.'

expectations.text: References full labeling and/or the confound between number of points and labeling
expectations.evidence: Response states: 'Labeling and point count are linked. You can fully label 5 points easily, 7 points with effort, and rarely more than that… A 7-point scale with every point labeled beats a 7-point scale with only endpoint labels. If you can't label all points clearly, don't add the points.'

claims.claim: Revilla, Saris & Krosnick (2014) found 5-category agree/disagree scales outperform 7- and 11-category on measurement quality
claims.evidence: This is an accurate description of the key finding of that paper.

eval_feedback.overall: No suggestions — the five assertions are well-chosen and all require substantive content to pass. Assertion 3 (does NOT simply agree) is a strong negative-direction check that prevents a low-effort agree-with-the-user response from passing.
